# fastf 3.4.0 — the template editor explains itself

A template is the thing that makes fastf worth installing: describe a folder
structure once and every project you make from it comes out the same way. The
editor for them was also the one screen that assumed you already knew what its
words meant.

It opened on five nouns — Metadata, ID, Variables, Structure, Files — with a
single line underneath, cut off with an ellipsis, as the whole of the
explanation. Everything else was in a 250-line document on GitHub, which is not
where you are when you are trying to build one.

## A panel that explains what you are looking at

Beside the list now is a panel that says what the highlighted part is, in
ordinary words, and shows **what your template would actually produce**:

- On **Metadata**, the folder name a project made from it would get:
  `2026-01-31_Ariana_Grande_Seeping_ID0001`. Change the pattern and it changes
  as you type.
- On **ID**, the first two numbers it would mint.
- On **Variables**, the questions it asks and the token each one gives you.
- On **Structure**, the folder tree, drawn.
- On **Files**, the documents it writes.

Open a part and the panel follows the field you are editing — what a slug is for
and why it may not contain spaces, what each transform does to a real answer,
why an ID prefix cannot be empty.

It is on by default. `i` hides it, and fastf remembers. On a window too narrow
for both, the list keeps the whole width and the one-line hint stays exactly
where it was.

## A guide, and a walkthrough that builds a real template

Press `G` on the templates tab or anywhere in the editor. Seven pages, written
for somebody who has not used the terminal app before:

- what a template is, and what is in one
- the five parts, and that nothing is written until you save
- how projects get their names: the pattern, the tokens, the ID
- the questions to ask: text, choices, defaults, transforms
- folders and files, and what gets filled in
- **build your first template** — a complete walkthrough with the values to type
- what happens after you save: where it lives, editing it, sharing it

`←` and `→` turn the page, Enter goes forward, Esc closes. Opened from a part of
the editor it lands on the page about that part, so it answers the question you
actually have.

fastf offers it **once**, unasked, the first time you open the templates tab or
the editor — whichever comes first, and never again. Esc leaves you exactly
where you were going.

## The editor says what is still missing

The Save row counts what is worth another look, and the panel names it: a
template with no name, a naming pattern that ignores its own variables, a
template that declares no folders and asks no questions.

**None of it stops you saving.** Every one of those is a template fastf will
load and use. They are listed because they are almost never what was meant — a
pattern that ignores its variables in particular asks you three questions,
records all three answers, and then gives every project the same folder name.

## Also

- The editor's own list now draws in the terminal's alphabet. On a console with
  no `·`, `…` or `→` — a legacy Windows one — the separator between a
  template's names, the "and so on" after its sample IDs, and the arrow in the
  transform examples were three replacement boxes.
- A hint too long for the editor's footer keeps its ellipsis. The line was
  measured one column wider than it was drawn, and the column that fell off the
  end was the one that said the sentence had been cut.
- The first-run welcome points at the templates tab and the guide.

Nothing changed about a flag, a config key or a file format. Every `config.toml`,
`template.yaml` and `PROJECT_INFO.md` an earlier fastf wrote still works, and
`state.toml` simply gains two remembered preferences.
